# Preface {-}

Are you ready to navigate the intersection of natural resources and computer science? This book is your guide to doing just that, equipping you with the essential skills to harness the power of data for forest management and conservation. More than just a collection of tools, this book provides a transparent and efficient approach to forestry informatics.

Through a hands-on, project-based approach, you'll learn to use the R programming language—a leading tool in data science and statistical analysis. You won't just be clicking buttons; you'll be writing code to:

    - Import and manage diverse forest inventory data.

    - Clean and analyze complex datasets to reveal key insights.

    - Create stunning visualizations that tell a clear story about your data.

By learning to use R command lines, you'll master a workflow that is not only powerful but also reproducible. This scientific approach ensures that your work is transparent, easily shared, and builds a foundation of credibility—a vital skill for any modern forester or natural resource professional. By the end of this book, you will be prepared to tackle the complex challenges facing our forests, equipped with the computational thinking and data-driven skills demanded by the industry.


![](fig/img1.png){width=5in }

## About this book {.unnumbered}

This short book should help you to get a better understanding of how the forest attributes analysis works, what you might want to consider in order to perform that are applicable for their respective purpose.

#Chapter 1: Introduction to Forest Data in R
Welcome to the foundation of our forestry visualization journey. Before we can generate beautiful maps or 3D canopy models, we must first import and prepare our field data. R is uniquely powerful for this, as it allows us to document our data-cleaning steps transparently and reproducibly.

In this chapter, we will set up our R environment, import our raw forest inventory data, and perform basic cleaning to ensure it is ready for spatial and statistical analysis.

#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Install packages if you haven't already: install.packages(c("tidyverse", "sf", "knitr"))
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(knitr) # Used for rendering neat tables in our book


<!--chapter:end:001-R_basic.Rmd-->

# Load Data {#load}

A forest inventory is a fundamental and comprehensive technical tool designed to collect as much information as possible about the status, composition, health, and productive potential of forest ecosystems.1 Unlike other assessment methods that may rely on remote sensing or large-scale modeling, field inventory is distinguished by its focus on direct data collection and in-situ measurements.2 This process not only generates detailed knowledge for sustainable management, but when carried out continuously in ten-year cycles, as in the Spanish National Forest Inventory, it allows the evolution of forest stands to be monitored over time.1 The methodology is based on sampling representative plots, which allows accurate estimates of key parameters to be obtained for vast geographical areas.2

We will use a data set published by Urquiza Muñoz et al,[@urquizamuñoz2021]. To start with, let's load and explore the data.

```{r load, message=FALSE, layout="l-body-outset"}
inventory <- read.csv("data/inventory_JDUM.csv")
```

In order to visualize the data in Rmarkdown, the following code will be employed:


```{r }
knitr::kable(head(inventory,10))
```


<!--chapter:end:002-load_data.Rmd-->

# Parts

You can add parts to organize one or more book chapters together. Parts can be inserted at the top of an .Rmd file, before the first-level chapter heading in that same file. 

Add a numbered part: `# (PART) Act one {-}` (followed by `# A chapter`)

Add an unnumbered part: `# (PART\*) Act one {-}` (followed by `# A chapter`)

Add an appendix as a special    kind of un-numbered part: `# (APPENDIX) Other stuff {-}` (followed by `# A chapter`). Chapters in an appendix are prepended with letters instead of numbers.




<!--chapter:end:03-parts.Rmd-->

## Citations

## Publishing

## 404 pages

By default, users will be directed to a 404 page if they try to access a webpage that cannot be found. If you'd like to customize your 404 page instead of using the default, you may add either a `_404.Rmd` or `_404.md` file to your project root and use code and/or Markdown syntax.

## Metadata for sharing

Bookdown HTML books will provide HTML metadata for social sharing on platforms like Twitter, Facebook, and LinkedIn, using information you provide in the `index.Rmd` YAML. To setup, set the `url` for your book and the path to your `cover-image` file. Your book's `title` and `description` are also used.


This `bs4_book` provides enhanced metadata for social sharing, so that each chapter shared will have a unique description, auto-generated based on the content.

Specify your book's source repository on GitHub as the `repo` in the `_output.yml` file, which allows users to view each chapter's source file or suggest an edit. Read more about the features of this output format here:

https://pkgs.rstudio.com/bookdown/reference/bs4_book.html

Or use:

```{r eval=FALSE}
?bookdown::bs4_book
```
